questions.q: Why is "Python is slow" usually the wrong diagnosis for a slow-running Python program?
options: Python has no interpreter overhead at all, so nothing in it can be slow
Most apparently slow Python code is actually spending its time inside already-compiled libraries like NumPy or pandas, not in the Python interpreter loop itself
Python code always runs faster than equivalent C++ code
Only code written before Python 3 can be slow
questions.explain: A lot of 'slow Python' is really time spent inside C/Fortran-backed libraries such as NumPy or pandas. Porting a thin Python wrapper around an already-fast call does not address the real bottleneck.

questions.q: A profiler shows 90% of a function's runtime inside a pure-Python, per-element loop. What should that tell you?
options: Nothing — profiler output should never influence a porting decision
This is a legitimate candidate for porting to C++, since the time is genuinely spent in interpreted, element-by-element work
The function should be deleted entirely
The loop should be rewritten in a different scripting language instead of C++
questions.explain: A hot path dominated by genuine Python-interpreted, element-by-element work is exactly the pattern worth porting to a compiled extension — profiling confirms the diagnosis before any rewrite effort is spent.

questions.q: Why can porting a tiny function like `double tinyFunction(double x) { return x * 2.0; }` and calling it from Python millions of times in a loop actually be a bad idea?
options: C++ cannot multiply floating-point numbers correctly
The per-call overhead of crossing the Python/C++ boundary, paid millions of times for trivial work each time, can dominate or exceed any speed gained from the computation itself
pybind11 limits every function to being called at most once
Doubles cannot be passed as function arguments in pybind11
questions.explain: Every call across the Python/C++ boundary has overhead. Paying that overhead millions of times for one multiplication each can cost more than it saves — the fix is to vectorize so the boundary is crossed once per batch, not once per element.

questions.q: What is the recommended way to port a per-path Monte Carlo simulation loop to C++ for the best performance gain?
options: Port only the single innermost arithmetic operation and call it once per path from Python
Port the entire per-path computation into C++ and call it vectorized, once per batch of paths, rather than once per path
Leave the loop in Python but add more print statements for visibility
Rewrite the loop as a Python generator instead of porting anything
questions.explain: Porting the whole loop and vectorizing the call amortizes the boundary-crossing overhead across the entire batch, instead of paying that overhead on every single call.

questions.q: Which scenario is the best candidate to leave in Python rather than port to C++?
options: A per-element pricing loop that profiling shows consumes 85% of total runtime on large inputs
A thin wrapper function that just calls `numpy.random.normal` and reshapes the result, run occasionally on small inputs
A Monte Carlo path simulator called millions of times with large batches
A function whose profile shows it as the single largest time consumer in the program
questions.explain: A thin wrapper around an already C-backed NumPy call, run rarely on small inputs, has no real bottleneck to fix — porting it adds build and maintenance overhead for no measurable gain.
